title: Water-Damaged Buildings and Health: An Updated Review of the Evidence, Sources of Bias, and Co-Occurring Conditions
content: Background. Water damage in buildings produces a mixture that includes fungi, bacteria, endotoxin, microbial fragments, and moisture-driven chemical emissions. The respiratory evidence has been graded; evidence on the multisystem symptoms many people report has been graded limited or inadequate, or not graded. Objectives. To summarize the evidence as of 2026; to examine how confounding, reporting bias, the composition of the exposure mixture, and co-occurring clinical conditions bear on the observed associations; and to propose a protocol for a rigorous future review. Methods. Structured evidence review (PubMed, Europe PMC, agency sources) with structured supplementary searches by body system and by exposure agent in November 2026 (145 database strategies); no registered protocol or duplicate screening. Results. The IOM and WHO graded no outcome as causal; two later reviews judged the evidence causal for asthma exacerbation in children, whereas a 2024 GRADE review rated effects in people with asthma uncertain. Pooled respiratory odds ratios are about 1.3 to 1.8, smaller in cohorts, and change modestly with socioeconomic adjustment. Measured agents such as endotoxin show both adverse and inverse associations. No epidemiological study of metabolic, hepatic, renal, endocrine, cardiovascular, or cancer outcomes, or of occupants' gut microbiome, was identified; these gaps indicate neither presence nor absence of an effect. No identified study systematically screened exposed people for bile acid malabsorption, iron deficiency, thyroid disease, sleep apnea, perimenopause, celiac disease, or postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome. HLA-DR typing has not been shown to provide diagnostic information. Conclusions. The respiratory and allergic evidence is sufficient to establish association. Beyond the airway, associations are reported for mental health, general symptoms, child neurodevelopment, skin, immune markers, and sarcoidosis, mostly in cross-sectional and self-reported designs; for metabolic, hepatic, renal, endocrine, cardiovascular, and cancer outcomes no epidemiological study was identified. The studies that would establish or exclude these associations have not been carried out, and tests used to assess exposure and susceptibility in an individual have not been validated for that purpose. The review sets out the design that research capable of answering these questions would require.
